# Crypto World's Fair: the complete Superteam Türkiye guide

Everything on https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum and the guides beneath it, as one document.

Generated from the site's own content on 2026-10-03. If a figure here disagrees with https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum, the site is right and this file is stale.

Written for people and for assistants. Paste the whole thing in and ask your question.

---

## The facts, stated once

- Competition: Crypto World's Fair, organised by Colosseum. Colosseum Org LLC administers it. Colosseum is an independent company, not a division or investment arm of the Solana Foundation.
- Format: online, global, and for the first time open to builders on every blockchain ecosystem.
- Building opened: 14 September 2026 at 06:00 Pacific, which is 16:00 in Türkiye. Section 5 of the official rules.
- Submission deadline: 12 October, 23:59 California time. That's 09:59 on 13 October in Türkiye.
- Every team member must register individually before 23:59 Pacific on 12 October or be disqualified. Section 6.
- Winners announced on or about 5 December 2026. Section 13.
- Prize pool: $840,000. This is not the same number as the venture fund.
- Venture fund: $2.5M, behind the accelerator. Accepted teams get $250,000 pre-seed and twelve weeks in San Francisco.
- Superteam Türkiye's own pool: 10,000 USDG, open only to teams based in Türkiye.
- All submission content must be in English. Section 12.
- Official rules: https://colosseum.com/legal/Crypto%20World's%20Fair%20Hackathon%20Rules.pdf
- Register (Superteam Türkiye referral): https://colosseum.com?ref=superteamtr-2026
- Our Earn listing: https://superteam.fun/earn/listing/submit-crypto-worlds-fair-project-for-turkish-builders/
- Our Telegram group: https://t.me/+3sWAzL4fgPViMjU8
- Our intake form: https://forms.gle/EELv1S3eD1nEytrq7
- Our calendar: https://luma.com/superteamtr

The two figures most often conflated are $840,000 and $2.5M. The first is prize money paid to placing teams. The second is venture capital deployed through the accelerator to a much smaller number of them.

The mistake that cannot be undone is the timezone. Colosseum runs on California time and Türkiye is ten hours ahead. A team that waits for midnight in Türkiye submits ten hours late.

## Not a coding contest. A pre-seed funnel.

Colosseum runs the largest hackathons in tech and then invests in the winning teams. Billed as a hackathon, judged as a seed round.

- **9,000+** Products submitted. Across Colosseum's competitions in two and a half years.
- **$60M** Fund I. Colosseum's own venture fund, backing the winners.
- **74** Portfolio startups. Funded out of the arena so far.
- **85%** Of VC-backed Solana startups. Colosseum's own number, published with this announcement.

### 01. The largest startup competition in tech
More products have been submitted here than to any other competition in crypto, and the company that runs it writes the cheques afterwards. It is one organisation doing both jobs, which is why placing well converts into capital rather than a certificate.

### 02. 85% of venture-backed Solana startups started here
If you want to raise in this ecosystem, this is the front door, not one of several. Teams that skip it end up pitching the same investors cold, a year later, without the proof.

### 03. Open to every chain, for the first time
All eight tracks are funded and published. Solana, Tempo, Hyperliquid and Zcash carry $100,000 each; Ethereum L1, Base, Arbitrum and Robinhood Chain carry $25,000. You pick up to three at registration, and every submission competes for the general awards as well, so a track is upside rather than a trade-off.

### 04. But the accelerator money is still Solana
Colosseum was explicit: the accelerator and venture fund keep investing in Solana founders. Build on Solana and you compete in your ecosystem track, in the cross-chain pool, and for the $250,000. Build elsewhere and the third one is not on the table.

### 05. Judges score you like investors, not graders
Founder-market fit, unique insight, execution quality, market size, communication, business model, and traction. Clean code is table stakes, not a score.

### 06. The field got harder on purpose
Colosseum's reasoning for opening it up: competition compounds. You are no longer measured against other Solana teams. You are measured against the best founders in crypto. Plan for that bar, not the old one.

## What's actually on the table.

$840,000 in prizes, and $2.5M of Colosseum's fund behind the teams that win. Every figure below is from the official rules, not the announcement.

- **$840,000** In prizes. Across the general awards and eight ecosystem tracks.
- **$2.5M** In seed funding. From Colosseum's venture fund, through the accelerator.
- **$250,000** Per accelerator team. Pre-seed, plus twelve weeks in San Francisco.
- **5 Dec** Winners announced. On or about 5 December, per the rules.

### Open to everyone

- **Grand Champion: $30,000.** One team. Paid in Phantom CASH.
- **The next 20 teams: $15,000 each.** $300,000 in total, and the band that feeds the accelerator.
- **Public Goods Award: $5,000.** One team.
- **University Award: $5,000.** One team.

### Pick up to three at registration

- **Solana: $100,000.** 10 products at $10,000
- **Tempo: $100,000.** 10 products at $10,000
- **Hyperliquid: $100,000.** 10 products, Hypercore or HyperEVM
- **Zcash: $100,000.** 10 products, chain or asset
- **Ethereum L1: $25,000.** 5 products at $5,000
- **Base: $25,000.** 5 products at $5,000
- **Arbitrum: $25,000.** 5 products at $5,000
- **Robinhood Chain: $25,000.** 5 products at $5,000

> **Read the two columns together**
> Track prizes are additive: every submission competes for the general awards too, whichever chain you chose. But the $2.5M behind this competition is the accelerator's, and Colosseum has been explicit that it still backs Solana founders. A Base team can win $5,000. A Solana team can win $5,000, the general pool, and a $250,000 cheque.

## A prize pool only Türkiye teams can win.

Colosseum organises its tracks per blockchain ecosystem, not per country, so there is no Türkiye track inside the competition itself. This runs alongside it on Superteam Earn, and it is additive: the project you enter for Colosseum's $840,000 competes here too.

- **10,000** USDG prize pool. On top of everything Colosseum pays.
- **Türkiye only** Who can enter. A regional listing. Your Colosseum profile has to say Turkey.
- **12 Oct** Same deadline. One project, two submissions, one clock.
- **28 Oct** Results. More than a month before Colosseum announces its own.

- 1st: 5,000 USDG
- 2nd: 3,000 USDG
- 3rd: 2,000 USDG

### Five things, and all five are checked

- Set Turkey as your primary base country on your Colosseum profile.
- Fill in the Superteam Türkiye intake form so we can track you and get you mentorship.
- Join the Colosseum hackathon group on Telegram.
- Submit the final project to both places: the Colosseum portal and this Earn listing. One is not the other.
- Include a pitch video (max 3 minutes), a demo video (max 3 minutes), and a public repository, or judges granted access if it stays private. Everything in English.

### What the local judges score

- Ecosystem impact. Does this add real infrastructure, tooling or value to Solana?
- Product-market fit on Solana. Is there genuine demand, and is there early traction to point at?
- User growth potential. Does it bring new people into the ecosystem, or deepen engagement for the ones already here?
- Presentation and adherence to the rules. Clarity of the videos, and strict compliance with the steps below.

> **This track is Solana, even though the competition isn't**
> Three of the four criteria name Solana explicitly. Crypto World's Fair is open to every ecosystem and this pool is not, so a team building elsewhere can still win Colosseum's general awards and its own ecosystem track, but not this one. It is the same split the accelerator makes, one scale down.

Hackathon tracks on Earn don't consume submission credits. Superteam Türkiye reserves the right to announce results later than 28 October if the volume of submissions needs more review time.
Listing: https://superteam.fun/earn/listing/submit-crypto-worlds-fair-project-for-turkish-builders/

## Week by week, start to submission.

Four weeks is enough for exactly one strong use case. This is where each week should end.

> **Before you follow the official guide**
> Colosseum's own How to Win guide was written for a five-week hackathon and tells you to spend four weeks engineering. This edition is four weeks. Give three to building, and give the whole last week to testing, the two videos and the submission.

### Every week until the deadline
Four fixed slots a week, all of them free and none of them compulsory. Subscribe once and the whole programme lands in your calendar.

- **Wednesdays · 19:00, Colosseum Community Call** (X Spaces). The week gets set here. One theme per call, and the room is where teams find each other.
- **Fridays · 10:00, Coworking Fridays** (Kolektif House Levent, İstanbul). In person, all day. Bring the thing you are stuck on.
- **Fridays · 19:00, Colosseum Office Hours** (Google Meet). One to one. Idea validation, architecture, deck and video review: whatever is blocking you that week.
- **Saturdays · 14:00, Shipyard** (Nişantaşı, and livestreamed). The vertical deep-dive. One place Solana actually wins, worked through properly.

**Community Calls** (Wednesdays, X Spaces)

- 16 Sep: Find Your Edge
- 23 Sep: Find Your Users
- 30 Sep: Reality Check
- 7 Oct: Fix What's Weak

**Shipyard** (Saturdays, İstanbul and livestream)

- 19 Sep: AI, Speed & Compute
- 26 Sep: RWA, Payments & Corridors
- 3 Oct: Gaming, Consumer & GTM

Calendar: https://luma.com/superteamtr

### Before Sep 14: Enter the arena and pick a fight
Goal: Register, build a team, and gap-check your idea.

- Create a Colosseum Arena account through Superteam Türkiye's referral link.
- Click Register in the upper-right corner and set your team location to Türkiye.
- Register even if you have no idea and no team yet. The project and team fields open on 14 September. Delaying costs you nothing but the invites and the office hours you'd have had in the meantime.
- Find teammates. Judges prefer teams of 3+. Solo entries are allowed, but harder.
- Run your idea through Colosseum Copilot against 5,400+ past projects. Full or partial gap: keep going. False gap: pivot now, not in week three.
- Fill in our orientation form so we know you're competing. It's what puts you on the list for kickoff sessions and office hours.
- Write a one-liner you can say out loud without apologizing for it.

### Week 1: Narrowest possible MVP
Goal: One user, one job, one screen that works on devnet.

- Cut scope until one use case works end to end. Overscoping is the single most common way Türkiye teams lose.
- Wire the chain integration early: wallet connect and a real transaction. If it can exist without a chain at all, judges notice.
- Use the existing stack instead of rebuilding it: Helius or Triton for RPC, Privy for auth, Jupiter for swaps, Squads for multisig, Pyth for prices.
- Post your first build-in-public update. Day one of a track record is better than day twenty.

### Week 2: Put it in front of humans
Goal: Real people used it and you have something to quote.

- Ship a public URL. A GitHub link isn't a demo.
- Get it in front of ten people who match your ideal customer and watch them use it, silently.
- Write down what broke. Fix what stops adoption; ignore what only annoys you.
- Start the pitch materials. Deck outline plus the story you'll tell on camera. Rough is fine. The structure isn't optional: Problem → Solution → Demo → Team.

### Week 3: Traction and narrative
Goal: Numbers on a slide and a story that explains them.

- Instrument the product. Users, retained users, transactions, volume. Pick the two you would defend to an investor.
- Build the narrative around the numbers, not around the vision.
- Record a rough pitch and watch it back at 1x. If the hook isn't in the first ten seconds, rewrite it.
- Ask Superteam Türkiye to amplify a real milestone. Not a launch announcement. A result.

### Week 4 · to Oct 12: Submission week
Goal: Everything uploaded two days early.

- The submit button unlocks 6 October, 4:00am PT. You can draft, save and edit your project on Colosseum before then, so there's no reason to wait for it to start writing.
- Pitch video, up to 2 minutes: problem, solution, team, traction. Founder voice, not a voiceover artist.
- Demo video, up to 3 minutes: the product doing the thing.
- Publish the repo. If it stays private, grant judges access. This is the most common disqualifying mistake.
- Submit the identical project to the Superteam Türkiye local listing.
- Know the deadline in your own timezone: 12 October, 23:59 California time. That's 09:59 on 13 October in Türkiye. Teams that assume midnight in Türkiye submit ten hours late.
- Submit two days early anyway. The platform is slow on the last night, every single time.

### After Oct 12: Don't stop
Goal: Momentum is a judging signal and a fundraising one.

- Keep shipping and keep posting. Judges fund teams that didn't treat the deadline as the finish line.
- Apply to the grant and accelerator ladder below.

---

## Nine things between you and a valid submission.

Every one of these has cost a team its submission before. Tick them off as you go. Your progress is saved in this browser.

- [ ] **One-liner and blurb written and reviewed.** One sentence a stranger understands without a follow-up question. (Send this to us before it goes live.)
- [ ] **MVP live on a public domain.** Publicly accessible. A localhost screenshot isn't a product.
- [ ] **Business and revenue model written down.** How this makes money, in three sentences. Judges score it explicitly. (Send this to us before it goes live.)
- [ ] **Your chain integration actually working.** Wallet connect and a real transaction, at minimum. Any ecosystem qualifies this time, but read the note on where the accelerator money sits before you choose.
- [ ] **Code published, or judges granted access.** Private repos and locked Google Docs are the most common own goal.
- [ ] **Verified X account, posting daily, following the judges.** The full panel is public now: five from Colosseum, plus fifteen track judges from Phantom, Base, Anza, Arcium, Drift, Ellipsis and MetaDAO. Follow them, and build in public. Silent teams read as abandoned.
- [ ] **Pitch materials drafted and reviewed.** Deck, pitch video and demo: one story told three ways, structured Problem → Solution → Demo → Team. Bring them to us rough; polishing before feedback wastes the week. (Send this to us before it goes live.)
- [ ] **Project and every team member registered on Colosseum.** Members missing from the project is a silent disqualifier.
- [ ] **Same project submitted to the Superteam Türkiye listing.** Identical project, submitted twice. The Colosseum portal and the Earn listing are separate places, and doing one is not doing the other.

## The playbook, in full

The 9 guides at https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/[slug], reproduced completely. These are the long-form answers; everything above is the summary. The last two are the same plan for people starting late, in English and in Turkish.

---

### 01. What judges actually score

*The seven official criteria, the AI that reads you before a human does, and what they explicitly don't grade.* (9 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/what-judges-score)

#### The seven criteria

Colosseum publishes what it evaluates. Almost nobody reads it, and it explains most losses.

- Founder-market fit and motivation: why you, specifically, for this problem.
- Unique insight and technology: what you know that the room doesn't.
- Product execution quality: does it work, and does it feel built.
- Market size: is the ceiling worth an investor's time.
- Founder communication: can you explain it in two minutes.
- Business viability: how it makes money.
- Traction and demand: proof someone wants it.

> **Read that list again**
> Five of the seven are business criteria. This is a startup competition wearing a hackathon's clothes.

- [The official rules, in full](https://colosseum.com/legal/Crypto%20World's%20Fair%20Hackathon%20Rules.pdf)

#### Something reads you before a human does

Colosseum runs an internal AI evaluation engine that filters submissions and raises flags before their team works through them. It scores founder-market fit, product velocity, user demand, market timing, and what they call evidence of grit in your past.

Humans still review afterwards. But something is reading your history before they reach you, and your history is not something you can build in four weeks, which is an argument for entering with the track record you already have, written down and linkable, rather than a clean slate.

After panel judging, a smaller group gets a fifteen-minute call. That call is about velocity and commitment, not a second demo. Expect to be asked what you shipped last week and whether you are doing this full time.

#### Two published criteria lists, and they disagree

The seven above are what Colosseum publishes in its own guidance. Section 8 of the official rules lists six different ones: functionality, potential impact, novelty, UX, open-source and composability, and business plan. Both are real, and where they conflict the rules are the document that settles an argument.

The sharpest conflict is about code. Colosseum's FAQ says they are not looking for a particular language or framework, or for design patterns, best practices, or code-quality checks, which is often quoted as "they don't grade your code". The rules say the opposite in the first criterion: "How well does this Project Submission work? What is the quality of the code?"

> **How to hold both**
> Nobody is marking your style. Something does have to work, and a judge who opens the repo has to be able to see that you built it and prioritised sensibly. Ship something functional, then stop. An extra week of refactoring buys you nothing that either list scores.

The rules also reward open-sourcing and composing with existing protocols directly, which the seven criteria never mention. If your repo is public and your product builds on other people's primitives, say so explicitly in the submission. It is a scored criterion, not a footnote.

#### Are you even eligible

Narrower than most people assume. This is for new startups that have not raised significant outside capital, and you are judged on work done inside the window. If you have already raised a round, read the rules before you spend four weeks on it.

#### Pitch and deck tactics

- The first ten seconds decide the rest. Judges review hundreds of submissions, so open with the problem and your solution, not with your team's origin story.
- People remember people, not PDFs. Record yourself. Let them feel the team.
- Slides support you, they don't speak for you. Less text, more clarity.
- Structure: Problem → Solution → Demo → Team. Deviating from this costs you clarity and buys you nothing.
- Scored does not mean it belongs in the video. Write the business model down where the form asks for it, and keep the three minutes for the problem, the product and the team. Revenue models and roadmaps read as padding at this length.

#### Show why your team matters

- Don't list names and titles. Say why each person is the right one to execute this specific thing.
- Link proof of execution: shipped products, repos, portfolios. Builders, not thinkers.

#### Product and audience

- If it's for everyone, it's for no one. A specific problem for a narrow audience beats a general product every time.
- Ship early, polish later. You don't have to be perfect to win, but you do have to be functional.

#### Further reading

- [How to Win a Colosseum Hackathon](https://blog.colosseum.com/how-to-win-a-colosseum-hackathon)
- [Perfecting Your Hackathon Submission](https://blog.colosseum.com/perfecting-your-hackathon-submission)
- [Hall of Fame: past winners](https://colosseum.com/arena/hackathon/hall-of-fame)

### 02. Validate before you build

*Run a gap analysis against 5,400+ past hackathon projects before you write a line of code. Takes an hour, saves three weeks.* (4 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/validate-your-idea)

#### The question that matters on day one

Has this been built before? If the answer is yes and you find out in week three, you have lost the hackathon. Colosseum ships a tool that answers it in an hour.

#### Setting up Colosseum Copilot

1. Generate a Personal Access Token in Arena.
2. Set COLOSSEUM_COPILOT_API_BASE and COLOSSEUM_COPILOT_PAT in your environment.
3. Install the skill into Claude Code or Codex: npx skills add ColosseumOrg/colosseum-copilot

> **The prompt**
> Validate this idea for the hackathon: [your idea]. Has anyone built this before, what is the competitive landscape, and what is genuinely unsolved?

#### Reading the answer

- False gap: already solved, and solved well. Pivot today.
- Partial gap: solved for a different audience or on a different chain. This is usually the best position to be in.
- Full gap: nobody has tried. Ask why before celebrating; sometimes there's a reason.

#### No idea yet?

Start from a problem list rather than a blank page. Our Türkiye request-for-proposals opens with registration; until then these are the best sources.

- [Superteam Idea Bank](https://superteam.fun/build/ideas)
- [Cofounder matching](https://colosseum.com/cofounder-matching)

---

### 03. Building AI-native on Solana

*Which chain to build on now that every ecosystem qualifies, and how to reach a working product on infrastructure that already exists.* (9 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/ai-native-solana-stack)

#### The rule

Every hour spent rebuilding something Helius or Privy already ships is an hour not spent on what judges actually score. Four weeks is enough for exactly one strong use case, and only if the plumbing is bought rather than built.

> **The test that decides your stack**
> If a hosted service exists and its free tier covers a hackathon's traffic, use it. Come back to the build-versus-buy question after you have users.

#### Which chain?

Crypto World's Fair is the first Colosseum competition open to every blockchain ecosystem, so this is a real decision now rather than a given. Prize tracks are organised per ecosystem (Solana, Tempo, Hyperliquid, Zcash, Ethereum L1, Base, Arbitrum and Robinhood Chain), and every submission also competes in a general pool across all of them.

> **The part that decides it for most teams**
> Colosseum's accelerator and venture fund keep investing in Solana founders. The hackathon opened up; the $250,000 did not. On Solana you're playing for your ecosystem track, the cross-chain pool and the accelerator. Anywhere else, the third one is off the table.

So the honest version: pick the chain your product actually needs. If the answer is genuinely another ecosystem (you need its liquidity, its users, its execution model), build there and compete for the prizes. If the answer is a coin flip, Solana is the one with money behind it after the competition ends, and it's the one we can help you with. Everything below is Solana-specific for that reason.

- Many strong entries will use more than one chain under the hood. Colosseum said as much in the announcement. Abstracting that away from users is a feature, not a hedge.
- Whatever you pick, judges ask why this chain. Have a real answer that names a property of the infrastructure, not a preference.

#### Start here, not from an empty repo

- solana.new: scaffolds plus the AI skills and MCP servers that let an agent write Solana code that compiles.
- Solana developer templates: working starting points for token, program, client and mobile projects.
- Solana Playground: browser-based build, test and deploy when you don't want to lose a morning to local toolchain setup.

- [solana.new: AI skills and scaffolds](https://www.solana.new/)
- [Solana developer templates](https://solana.com/developers/templates)
- [Superteam developer tools](https://superteam.fun/build/developer-tools)
- [Superteam Build: resources](https://superteam.fun/build/resources)

#### The Solana SaaS stack

The pieces below are what production Solana teams actually run. Picking from this list isn't cutting corners; it's the same decision the companies you're competing against already made.

- RPC and transaction landing: Helius, Triton, Jito bundles. Don't ship on a public endpoint; dropped transactions during a demo are unrecoverable.
- Wallet authentication: Privy. Email and social login onto a real wallet, which is usually the difference between a demo people finish and one they abandon.
- Swaps and routing: Jupiter Ultra.
- Multisig and smart accounts: Squads Protocol and their APIs.
- Rollups and compression: Magicblock, Light Protocol.
- Prices and oracles: Pyth, Switchboard.

- [Solana transaction guide: why yours isn't landing](https://www.solanatransaction.com/)
- [Solana developer documentation](https://solana.com/developers)
- [Solana Stack Exchange: when the agent and the docs both fail you](https://solana.stackexchange.com/)

#### Learning it fast enough to matter

If you're arriving from another ecosystem, don't read the whole documentation set. Take one guided path end to end, then build.

- [Blueshift: the best structured Solana course](https://blueshift.gg/)
- [Superteam hackathon headquarters](https://superteam.fun/hackathon)

#### AI-native means the product, not the pitch

Saying your product uses AI isn't a differentiator in 2026; every submission says it. AI-native means the core loop is impossible without a model: the agent is the product, not a feature bolted onto a dashboard.

1. Remove the model. Does the product still exist? If yes, you have an AI feature, not an AI-native product.
2. Remove Solana. Does it still work on a normal database? If yes, judges will say so before you do.
3. If both removals break it, you have found the thing worth building for four weeks.

The places the two genuinely need each other are agentic payments, autonomous onchain execution, and verifiable memory or provenance. Everything else tends to be a web app with a chat box.

#### Using AI to build, not just to demo

- Install the Solana skills for your coding agent from solana.new before you write anything. An agent without them will confidently produce Solana code that doesn't compile.
- Run Colosseum Copilot alongside them for competitive context, not just code.
- Review what the agent writes against the transaction guide. Programs that work on devnet and fail under real load are a common and very visible way to lose a demo.

### 04. Narrative, and building in public

*Used strategically, X measurably improves your odds. How to run it as a feedback loop rather than a megaphone, including what the algorithm rewards and what it flags.* (7 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/narrative-and-building-in-public)

#### Why narrative is a judging criterion in disguise

Founder communication is scored explicitly, and traction is scored right after it. Both are downstream of whether you can explain what you're doing in a way people repeat. If you use X strategically over these four weeks, your chances of winning go up measurably, not because judges count followers, but because everything they do score gets easier when people already know what you're building.

> **It isn't marketing**
> Building in public is the cheapest way to find out you're building the wrong thing while there's still time to change it. The feedback is the product of the exercise; the audience is a side effect.

#### Two accounts, two jobs

Run the project and yourself as separate voices. They reinforce each other and the split stops either from becoming noise.

- Project account: releases, new features, progress, and replies. What shipped, what broke, what's next.
- Personal account: opinions, insight, and replies. The thinking behind the product, not its changelog.
- Both reply and like daily. Visibility here is mostly a function of being present in other people's threads.

#### What the algorithm rewards

- Subscribe to X Premium. It changes reach materially.
- Attach an image or video. Posts without media are throttled against posts with them.
- Put links in a reply to your first post, never in the post itself.

That last one is the rule people break most, and it's the most expensive. A link in the first post caps its distribution before anyone sees it. Post the thought, then reply to yourself with the link.

#### What gets you flagged

- Don't buy followers. It's a red flag, and it's visible to anyone who looks at your ratios.
- Don't pay influencers. Judges and investors read it exactly as what it is.
- Don't use hashtags.
- Don't fill a post with blue text: stacked mentions and links suppress reach.
- Don't put a link in the first post.

#### One sentence, repeated

Pick the sentence in week one and don't change it. It goes in your bio, your first slide, your pitch video's opening line, and every post. Repetition is what turns a project into a thing people can refer to when you aren't in the room.

- Name the problem, not the technology.
- Say who it's for inside the sentence.
- If it needs a second sentence to make sense, it isn't the sentence yet.

#### Cadence

- Start on day one. Twenty small posts across four weeks is a track record; twenty in the final week is noise.
- Post results, not intentions. "Shipped X, here's what broke" outperforms "excited to announce" every time.
- Follow the judges. Cheap, and it works.

#### Where we amplify

Superteam Türkiye will amplify shipped milestones: a working demo, a real user number, a launch. We won't amplify an announcement that you have started. Bring us the result and we'll put it in front of the ecosystem.

- [Build in public, worked through in a thread](https://x.com/mxmnci/status/1940478798178439654)

---

### 05. The submission itself

*What to upload, in what format, why the video matters more than the deck, and the two rules that get teams disqualified.* (8 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/submission)

#### The package

- Project description and team details.
- Pitch video, up to 2 minutes, public on your project page. This one explains the why: who you are, what it does, why you started, the market, how you get customers, and a working demo.
- Demo video, up to 3 minutes, a separate upload. This one explains the how. Keep it technical. It is not a second pitch, and turning it into one wastes the only slot where a judge watches the thing actually run.
- GitHub repository with the hackathon code.
- Go-to-market notes, logo, and team location. Set the location to Türkiye.

There is also a weekly one-minute update video Colosseum asks for. It is optional on paper and most teams skip it, which is exactly why it works: it is the cheapest evidence of momentum you can produce, and they watch them.

#### Build the video first, not the deck

Superteam Balkan went through all 139 winning submissions from the past three hackathons and counted what each team actually uploaded. Around 88% were a recorded video rather than a static deck: 63 Loom, 49 YouTube, 8 Vimeo, against roughly 16 PDFs. The Grand Champion submitted a YouTube video.

Colosseum's own line is that the pitch video is usually the first item judges review and can decide whether a project is shortlisted at all. Standard startup advice says the opposite and warns founders off video, but that advice is written for a live demo day with five hundred people in the room. This is one reviewer working alone through a hundred submissions. In that setting the video does the job the deck would.

> **Whose numbers these are**
> The 139-submission count is Superteam Balkan's own research, not a Colosseum statistic. We are using it because nobody else has done the work.

- [Superteam Balkan's write-up of the count](https://x.com/solanamarko/status/2098084013332210127)
- [Their full hackathon guide](https://stblkn.notion.site/colosseum-hackathon)

#### The one-liner might be the whole thing

A good one-liner gets you shortlisted on its own. It is what a judge remembers an hour later, and what an investor repeats to their partners when you are not in the room. "Stablecoin neobank for SMBs" survives being repeated by someone who does not care about your product. Most one-liners do not.

#### Five rules for every slide

1. Write the takeaway in the title. Never put "Problem" at the top of a slide. Put "Users lose $4M a year to wallet drains."
2. One point per slide.
3. Under 40 words. Past that, reviewers skim.
4. Cut the superlatives. Every founder writes revolutionary and fastest. Replace them with proof: start to finish in 15 seconds, $400 saved per user per month.
5. Every slide readable in 15 seconds. Assume 90 seconds for the whole deck.

#### Four ways to lose after doing the work

- Overselling the future. A grand vision with no track record reads as a pitch, not a product. Show the MVP.
- Forced crypto integration. If the product could exist without a chain, your use of one has to be justified deeply, or not claimed at all.
- A weak demo. A repository link isn't a demo. There must be something a judge can watch working.
- Missing permissions. Private repos and locked Google Docs that judges can't open. This is the single most common fatal mistake. If your repo stays private, grant access to hackathon@colosseum.com, then have someone outside your team confirm they can actually open every link you submitted.

#### Two rules that get teams disqualified

These are not style points. Both have removed teams from competitions that had already done the work.

1. One product per team, and one per person. You cannot submit two projects, and you cannot appear on two submissions.
2. You may start before the window opens and reuse your own code, but only work done inside the window is judged, and you have to disclose all prior development on the submission form.

> **What happens if you don't disclose**
> Colosseum's own words: they disqualify the team, ban the builders from future hackathons, and revoke prizes. Disclosing prior work costs you nothing. Teams with a running start have placed well. Hiding it costs you everything.

Building on other people's open source is fine and actively encouraged. The pre-existing code rule is about your own earlier work, not about the libraries and protocols you compose with.

#### Timing

Submit two days early. Every hackathon has a slow final night, and there's no appeal for a deadline missed by ten minutes.

---

### 06. After the deadline

*Grants, accelerators, and Eternal: with real terms. The funding ladder for teams that shipped something real, whether or not they placed.* (5 min, https://tr.superteam.fun/colosseum/after-the-hackathon)

#### Momentum is a signal

The hackathon doesn't end on submission day. Judges and investors both look at what a team did in the two weeks after the deadline, because that's when the ones who were only there for the prize stop.

#### Almost nobody wins their first one

Unruggable entered four Colosseum hackathons: an honourable mention at Renaissance, another at Radar, a first-place track win at Breakout, then the Grand Championship at Cypherpunk. Colosseum built a section of their own site around this, under the line that the best builders don't just compete once.

The threshold is also higher up the table than most people assume. Placing in the top group is what feeds the accelerator, so aim there rather than at the single top spot, and if you place nowhere, the useful question is what you enter next, not whether you were right to enter at all.

#### Accelerators

- [Colosseum Accelerator: $250K on founder-friendly terms, and the hackathon is the only way in](https://colosseum.com/accelerator)
- [Colosseum Eternal: self-paced 4-week sprint, $25K USDC. Paused; expected back around November](https://colosseum.com/eternal)
- [Alliance DAO: $500K for around 7%](https://alliance.xyz)
- [Orange DAO Fellowship: $100K MFN SAFE](https://www.orangedao.xyz)
- [Monke Foundry](https://www.monkedao.io)

#### Grants

- [Solana Foundation grants](https://solana.org/grants-funding)
- [Solana Mobile builder grants](https://solanamobile.com)
- [Circle developer grants](https://www.circle.com/blog/circle-developer-grants)
- [Superteam Earn: grants and bounties](https://superteam.fun/earn)

If you shipped something real during the hackathon, you're also a credible Superteam Türkiye membership applicant. That's the door to local grants and perks.
